analysis.one_liner: Bars risky fees and terms like balloon payments and prepayment penalties on high-cost home equity loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; it was referred to committee, held one subcommittee hearing in March 1994, and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to protect homeowners who take out high-cost loans secured by their homes. Lenders would have to plainly warn borrowers they could lose their home, and loans could no longer include prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, or fees for refinancing with the same lender. It would let borrowers recover all finance charges and fees from lenders who break the rules, let state attorneys general sue to enforce the law, and make investors who buy these loans responsible for claims against the original lender. It also preserves states' power to set their own caps on interest and fees for home equity loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners — often older, lower-income, or less financially sophisticated borrowers — who pledge their homes to borrow money at high rates and heavy fees. The disclosures, banned loan terms, and expanded damages would make it harder to strip their equity through costly loan structures, and assignee liability would follow the loan even if it is sold to investors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners taking high-cost home equity loans

how_it_helps.text: Lenders must disclose in plain language, three business days before closing, that the borrower could lose the home and all money put into it, and must state that the borrower may be able to get a less expensive loan elsewhere.

High-cost mortgages may not include prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, or more than two payments consolidated and prepaid from loan proceeds, and refinancing with the same lender or an affiliate cannot charge new points and fees on the refinanced portion.

If a lender violates the requirements, the borrower can recover all finance charges and fees, not just statutory penalties, and state attorneys general can sue to enforce the rules within five years of a violation.

Investors who buy or are assigned a high-cost mortgage are subject to all claims and defenses the borrower could raise against the original lender, which discourages the secondary market from buying abusive loans.

States keep their authority to limit interest, fees, and other terms on first-lien home equity loans under two federal preemption statutes, so state-level protections cannot be wiped out by federal law.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost home equity lenders, mortgage brokers whose commissions were financed into loans, and investors who buy these loans on the secondary market. They lose banned fee income and gain legal exposure: the bill adds full fee-and-finance-charge damages, attorney general enforcement, and assignee liability. Home improvement contractors face new limits on how funds are disbursed and paid.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-cost home equity lenders and mortgage brokers

drawbacks.text: The rules apply only to 'high cost' loans — those exceeding a Treasury-rate spread by more than 10 points or with points and fees above 8 percent of the amount financed (with a $400 floor) — so lenders could stay outside the rules by pricing loans just under the thresholds.
The bill reaches only loans secured by a principal dwelling that are not home purchase mortgages, so other costly mortgage products remain uncovered.

Banning prepayment penalties and restricting refinancing fees on high-cost loans could make this credit more expensive or harder to get for borrowers with weak credit, since lenders have less way to recoup early payoffs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target real, documented loan structures that strip home equity from vulnerable borrowers: banning balloon payments and negative amortization on home equity loans, and forcing plain-English warnings that the house is at risk, are low-cost safeguards. The honest trade-off is that the rules could raise prices or reduce availability of credit for the highest-risk borrowers at the margin, and the thresholds leave room for loans priced just under them. On balance, the equity-protection benefits for homeowners outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Banking Committee after referral, got one subcommittee hearing in March 1994, and died without ever being reported or voted on when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph P. Kennedy II introduced the bill on September 28, 1993, with 25 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
On October 18, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Credit and Insurance.
The subcommittee held a hearing on March 22, 1994, but the committee never reported the bill and the full House never voted on it before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost home equity lenders, mortgage brokers, and loan purchasers, who continued operating without the disclosure rules, banned loan terms, and assignee liability the bill would have imposed. Homeowners taking these loans kept bearing the risks the bill aimed to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost home equity lenders and loan buyers

industries.industry: High-cost home equity and subprime mortgage lenders
industries.note: The bill bans prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, and prepaid-payment structures on high-cost home equity loans, and lets borrowers recover all finance charges and fees for violations. These are the fee income and loan structures such lenders relied on, and the industry's interest in keeping them runs against homeowners' equity.

The bill requires a separate written contract stating the broker's commission before application and prohibits financing broker commissions otherwise, cutting into how brokers were paid on high-cost loans.

industries.industry: Loan purchasers and the secondary mortgage market
industries.note: Assignees of high-cost mortgages become liable for all claims and defenses the borrower could assert against the original lender, with relief capped at offsetting remaining debt plus amounts paid, making these loans riskier to buy.

The bill limits advance disbursements to no more than 80 percent of funds on contracts over $10,000 before work is completed and requires joint-payee instruments, curbing contractor-fronted financing but also giving consumers new protections against paying for unfinished work.
